No—Albert Einstein **did not win the Nobel Prize for relativity** (neither special nor general relativity). He was awarded the **1921 Nobel Prize in Physics** (awarded in 1922) **“for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.”**

The photoelectric effect work—published in 1905 as part of his “Annus Mirabilis” (Miracle Year) papers—was pivotal in establishing quantum theory. Einstein proposed that light consists of discrete packets of energy (later called *photons*), and that electrons are ejected from a material only when struck by light above a certain frequency—a concept that classical wave theory couldn’t explain.

While relativity revolutionized physics, it remained controversial and less empirically confirmed at the time (e.g., the 1919 eclipse confirmation of general relativity was still recent and debated). The Nobel Committee, cautious about awarding for theories perceived as speculative, chose the photoelectric effect—a discovery with clear experimental support and profound implications for quantum mechanics.

So, to clarify:  
✅ Nobel Prize: Yes (1921, awarded 1922)  
✅ For the photoelectric effect: Yes  
❌ For relativity: No  

It’s a common misconception—but an important one to get right! 😊
